stemBlocks.value: A shop sells notebooks, pens and rulers on Monday and Tuesday. The quantity matrix Q = (8 12 5 / 10 9 7) has row 1 for Monday and row 2 for Tuesday, and the price matrix p = (6 / 3 / 4) gives the price in dollars of a notebook, a pen and a ruler. (a) State why the product Qp is defined. (b) Calculate Qp. (c) Interpret each element of Qp in the context of the question.
Think first: Multiplying quantities by prices in the right order gives money, and the row-by-column rule does the whole calculation in one go.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p202-q16 from workbook page 202.

solutionSteps.instruction: Compare the columns of Q with the rows of p.

contentBlocks.value: Q is 2 × 3 and p is 3 × 1; the inner numbers are both 3.

solutionSteps.instruction: Multiply the Monday row into the price column.
Multiply the Tuesday row into the price column.
Write the product as a column and attach the meaning.

contentBlocks.value: Each entry pairs quantities with the matching prices and adds.

strategyBlocks.value: Check that the 3 columns of Q match the 3 rows of p, multiply each day's row into the price column, then read the answers as money.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) Q has 3 columns and p has 3 rows; since these agree, Qp is defined and has order 2 × 1  (b) Qp = (104 / 115)  (c) The first element, 104, is the total money in dollars taken on Monday; the second element, 115, is the total money in dollars taken on Tuesday.

whyThisWorks.value: Each entry of Qp multiplies every quantity by the price of that same item and adds the results, which is exactly how a shop totals a day's takings. Putting the prices in a column is what lines each price up with its own column of quantities. If the price matrix were written as a row, the product would not be defined at all.

examTip.value: In a costing question, arrange quantities as rows and prices as a column — the shape then guarantees the arithmetic pairs correctly.
